svg.title: DDIA 9 · THE TROUBLE WITH DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS: sketchnote
svg.text: DDIA 9 · THE TROUBLE WITH DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS
Partial failure: some parts work, some don't, and you often can't tell which. Networks, clocks and pauses all lie.
From the client's side, all three look IDENTICAL: a timeout
The client only knows "no reply before the timeout". That is
why every retried operation must be idempotent.
Last-write-wins compares timestamps, and the causally later
write loses. No error is raised. NTP accuracy is only tens of ms
write file (thinks it holds the lock!)
Client 1 wakes up, checks nothing, and writes. Two writers
A late writer with an old token is rejected. The protection is
enforced by the resource, not trusted to the client.
One process, one thread, simulated time
Fake network · fake clock · fake disk
Run every node in one seeded simulator with fake network,
clock and disk. Any failure replays exactly from its seed.
"What if the payment provider times out?"
Outcome unknown. Retry with the same idempotency key, or reconcile with a status query. Never blindly charge again.
Fine for efficiency (avoid duplicate work). For correctness add fencing tokens, or use the DB's own conditional writes.
Wall clocks skew. Use a sequence from one leader, a Kafka partition offset, or logical clocks (Ch 9).
"How do you detect a dead node?"
Heartbeats + timeouts tuned to p99.9, and accept false positives. Leader election by majority, with epochs to fence the old leader.
Study notes on Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition (Kleppmann & Riccomini). Read the book.
